item.title: Target Earnings: The ‘Target Run’ Is Making a Comeback
item.description: When Target Corp. named long-serving executive Michael Fiddelke to succeed Brian Cornell as chief executive officer a year ago, he had two tasks.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Felsted

item.title: Florida Primary Results: Democrats Make Things Harder for Themselves
item.description: Florida demonstrated on Tuesday that the Democratic Party’s identity crisis is alive and well. It’s the latest signal that while the midterm election will be a referendum on the president’s performance, it’s also a major test of the Democratic Party’s ability to bridge its growing divide.
item.dc:creator: Mary Ellen Klas

item.title: Mark Walter’s Lakers Sale Highlights Modern Sports Ownership Risks
item.description: Mark Walter should be precisely the kind of owner the National Basketball Association wants. He is spectacularly wealthy and — as he’s proved as the owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers — he’s willing to spend big to win.
item.dc:creator: Adam Minter

item.title: RFK Jr.’s Impact on Kindergarten Vaccine Rates Seen in CDC Data
item.description: In an early but damning gauge of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s impact since his ascent to US health secretary, a growing number of Americans are sending their kids off to kindergarten without crucial vaccines.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Jarvis

item.title: The Decline in Murder Is Clear. The Reason Is Not
item.description: “Every single number is the lowest number in recorded history,” President Donald Trump said while unveiling the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 2025 US crime report last week. It may not be surprising to learn that this was false: Despite falling sharply in 2025, the population-adjusted rate of aggravated assaults — one of the four main violent crimes tracked by the FBI — was still higher than in the early 2010s. So was the rate of rapes, albeit mainly because of definitional changes made in 2
item.dc:creator: Justin Fox

item.title: Malaria-Carrying Mosquitoes Have a New Foe in Science and Genetics
item.description: Almost half a million children under the age of 5 die of malaria each year. What if replacing a single amino acid in disease-carrying mosquitoes could help save them? After battling with rudimentary tools for millennia, malaria fighters are now armed with a potentially revolutionary technology. If only the public could get on board.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Apple Must Heed the Lessons of Meta’s ‘Pervert’ Glasses
item.description: In what looks like a curiously sloppy oversight, Apple Inc. has inadvertently confirmed Bloomberg’s reporting on the company’s first big swing at an AI-enhanced wearable device. Hidden in a coming Mac software update, a 13-second video shows a man wearing AirPods pick up a book and hold it in front of him. “With Visual Intelligence,” the voice-over says, “your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.”
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: Harvard Needs Honest Grading to Preserve Its Academic Credibility
item.description: University policies on grades, like grades themselves, run along a wide spectrum. Harvard, my alma mater and my employer, wants to combat grade inflation and so is limiting the number of A’s in undergraduate classes. Michigan, meanwhile, wants to combat grade anxiety and so is eliminating grades altogether for first-year students in their first semester.
item.dc:creator: Noah Feldman

item.title: The $19 Trillion Bond Question Confronting Central Banks
item.description: We all care about the interest rates that central banks set, but what about the $19 trillion of bonds and other assets held by the biggest among them? Those constitute a more esoteric, but equally consequential, element of monetary policy that’s lately transcended the wonky to become politically fractious. item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: Sentiment: Fund Managers Are Acting Like Summer Will Never End
item.description: The latest optimism seems out of sync with both oil and the midterms.
item.dc:creator: John Authers

item.title: A FIFA Boycott Would Punish Women Footballers First
item.description: When football organizations around the world put their heads together to find a solution to the problem of Gianni Infantino, they came up with one answer: a boycott. While the drastic measure may be the strongest card they have to play, it’s women — not FIFA — who would pay the immediate price.
item.dc:creator: Emily Nicolle

item.title: The Mecca Pact Is No ‘Sunni NATO.’ But It’s a Start
item.description: It might be hard to imagine that the Middle East is looking beyond Washington at the precise moment it is being massively disrupted by a US-led war. But that is exactly what’s happening – most recently through this month’s signing of the Mecca Agreement, a mutual defense pact between Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey and Shehbaz Sharif of Pakistan.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Sharma

item.title: Thiel-Backed Erebor Bank Wants to Echo SVB. That’s Risky
item.description: A dragon’s lair isn’t where most people would stash their cash, even in fantasy fiction. But that’s not slowing down the real-world Erebor Bank — named after the mountain home of a treasure-hoarding beast in JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit. The tech-focused lender, founded by Palmer Luckey and backed by Peter Thiel, wants to conquer the market Silicon Valley Bank dominated before it collapsed in 2023. That’s not necessarily a bright idea.
item.dc:creator: Paul J. Davies

item.title: As the US Juggles Wars in Iran and Ukraine, North Korea Is a Wildcard
item.description: The US military can generally handle one major crisis, and even a second challenge, but a third would stretch its capacity.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: We’re Having the Wrong Debate About AI Safety
item.description: China’s embrace of open-source artificial intelligence is giving Silicon Valley a run for its money. It’s also become a major source of clout for Beijing, luring international developers and emerging as a cornerstone of President Xi Jinping’s pitch for collaboration with the Global South and influence over the next tech revolution.
item.dc:creator: Catherine Thorbecke

item.title: Why Zhu Rongji's Death Has Made China Wistful for the 1990s
item.description: The death of a beloved leader has often presented challenges for China’s ruling Communist Party. With few avenues for overtly criticizing the regime, public mourning can become an expression of broader discontent.
item.dc:creator: Juliana Liu

item.title: Under Trump, America's Pivot to Asia Takes a U-Turn
item.description: Lacking a coherent or even discernible strategy in geopolitics, Donald Trump has inadvertently reversed the direction in which American foreign and security policy was going for the past three presidential administrations, including his first. Two more veers took place this week in Asia.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kluth

item.title: South Korea Makes Billions, and Takes Home Little
item.description: South Korea, home to the world’s two-largest memory chipmakers, is in the midst of an AI-fueled exports boom. Generating wealth and keeping it at home isn’t the same thing, however.
item.dc:creator: Shuli Ren

item.title: Texas Municipal Bonds Are Paying the Price for Anti-ESG Legislation
item.description: “Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall. Humpty Dumpty had a great fall. All the king's horses and all the king's men couldn't put Humpty together again.”
item.dc:creator: Matthew A. Winkler
